task: Write one sentence of your own using the word mendacious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know mendacious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Fact-checkers counted eleven mendacious claims in the celebrity's twelve-minute interview.
Mistaken stops far short of mendacious — a mistaken witness is wrong without meaning to be.
Misleading stops short of mendacious — a misleading claim bends true facts, while a mendacious one invents them.

Deceitful accuses someone of practicing deception of any kind — in word or act, a tipped scale as much as a spoken lie. Mendacious is narrower and sharper: mendacious deception lives in words, in statements deliberately false. Every mendacious speaker is deceitful, but deceit needs no sentences at all.

Untruthful is the mild, careful way to accuse someone of false statements — a report might call testimony untruthful where a tabloid would say lying. Mendacious levels the same words-based charge at full force, insisting the falsehoods are deliberate. Both point at statements, not at tricks or props.
telling things as they are
upright in word and dealing alike
Reviewers accused the memoir of mendacity within a week of its release.
Mendacious means deliberately untruthful; lying.

The 'haunted lighthouse' pamphlet sold in the gift shop is cheerfully mendacious: the keeper it mourns never existed, the shipwreck it describes happened in another country, and the 'original logbook' on display was printed the year the shop opened.
Mendacious is stronger than 'misleading' because it accuses the source of deliberate lies, not sloppy errors—a mistaken guide gets the facts wrong; a mendacious one invents them on purpose.
Mendacious is a formal accusation of deliberate lying — auditors, historians, and editorials use it when 'inaccurate' would be too kind.
Its unit-mate perfidious accuses something different: the mendacious lie in what they say, while the perfidious betray a trust they still pretend to keep.

The bestselling autobiography of motivational speaker Dade Harmon ran ninety pages and, as the Ledger discovered, contained roughly forty true ones.
The ultramarathon he claimed to have won did not exist; the race did not either.
The 'engineering degree' was a weekend certificate.
The 'family farm' was a rental cottage his parents once photographed in autumn.

What made the book mendacious rather than merely embellished, the Ledger argued, was the paper trail: Harmon had corrected the ghostwriter's accurate first draft by hand, inserting each invention himself, in green ink.
Asked for comment, Harmon said he stood by 'the spirit of the text.' The Ledger printed the green-ink pages the next morning.
